newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany braced for fresh debate on short work week.
newsitem.headline: Germany braced for fresh debate on short work week.

text.p: Germany looks poised to enter a fresh round of wrangling over working hours after the country's largest union proposed yet another cut in the already short work week in a bid to create new jobs.

Following a policy pursued since the late 1980s, the IG Metall union said on Wednesday it wanted to roll back the work week in the crucial engineering sector to 32 hours. The last cut-back, to 35 hours from 40, has yet to be fully implemented.

Evoking a ground-breaking deal struck at carmaker Volkswagen AG in late 1993 -- which set a 28.8 hour week to save jobs at VW's German plants -- IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel said individual workers in the sector could also work just four days a week.
Reducing hours to give workers more leisure time was a union rallying cry in the late 1980s. The idea of opening up the possibility of creating more jobs seemed like an afterthought.

But as Germany's employment problems intensified in the 1990's despite a short-lived growth boom fuelled by German unification, this approach turned into the labour groups' main strategy to cut jobless queues.
"We threw existing pay contracts into the ring in exchange for working hours," IG Metall negotiator Juergen Peters said of the then-unique Volkswagen deal struck in November 1993.
Later attempts to achieve similar deals on a country-wide basis plunged Germany into months of agonised debate.

The talks, conducted most publicly in last year's "Alliance for Jobs" round-table hosted by Chancellor Helmut Kohl, failed to reconcile the union goal of reducing work hours and overtime and the employers' need for flexibility and cheaper labour.

Independent economists warned on Wednesday that relaunching the debate could be dangerous at a time when well-paid, well-vacationed German industry struggles to keep pace in an increasingly competitive global trading environment.
"This proposal is an extension of the line the unions have taken since the 1980's," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.

"The problem is that it is based on the mistaken belief that there is a fixed quantity of work that can just be redistributed. The fact is that if conditions are appropriate then the economy will grow and employment will rise.
"Zwickel's proposal is just a dead-end street."

The union proposal comes as doubts are growing about the continued success of the "German economic model" driven by a high level of consensus between unions and management coupled with a high level of wealth distribution and job security.
This approach, which proved spectacularly successful rebuilding post-war West Germany, has become cumbersome in today's faster-moving business world.

"Adding more employees, which is not possible to an unlimited extent anyway, would also mean cost-intensive training and additional worker participation dicussions as the company grows as a result," said Ralf Kugelstadt at UBS.
"It is hard to see where the benefit for the company lies."

The rigid labour market structures, which make it extremely costly to dismiss any employee after just two years with a firm, stand in sharp contrast to Britain and the United States, which have had greater success in creating jobs.
The United States alone has created over 11 million jobs in the last four years.
Rejecting the IG Metall proposal out of hand, engineering employers' group Gesamtmetall made a clear reference to such successes, saying these had not been achieved by working less.
"Nowhere in the world is a cut in working time used as a means in the battle against unemployment," Gesamtmetall said.
"A general cut in working time has been consciously avoided in precisely those countries which have been more successful than Germany in maintaining and creating jobs," it added.

With the country seemingly headed for another fruitless debate, Goldman Sachs' Mayer said the unions' should take their cue from counterparts abroad and stop clinging to cosy but out-dated structures if a real solution were to be found.

"The general problem that we have in this country is that left-wing parties and the trade unions are stil years behind the developments that left-wing parties and unions have taken in other countries," Mayer said.
